card.adopted: none

card.say: At Debon Securities, I was moving part of our trading app to the new navigation. During testing I found some old pages had a broken back button. I told the project manager that same day, before I had checked every page. I gave two options: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and test the rest after. He decided to keep the old pages, so everything else shipped on time. I finished the fix and the testing myself, and my change went out in the next release.

updates: He decided to keep the old pages, so everything else shipped on time. I finished the fix and the testing myself, and my change went out in the next release. If he had refused to delay, I'd have explained the risk clearly: which pages could break and for how many users. Then I'd ask for a quick way to turn the change off. The decision is his, but my job is to make the risk clear.

The pages I found were older, low-traffic ones. If the broken back button had been on the checkout flow, I would have pushed harder to delay the release. I wouldn't have offered the ship-and-test-later option at all.

turns.question: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. turns.question: You said the repository saves the intent with its client transfer ID in the local database before calling the server. On Android, how is that local write actually done so it's durable before the network call, and what exactly gets stored in that row?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: Client layers (Screen, ViewModel, Repository, Local DB) talk to the server API, which owns the ledger; local DB caches balance and history and saves the transfer intent before sending

card.heard: how is that local, what gets stored in that row
card.say: The repository writes the intent row to Room on the IO dispatcher, and it waits for that write to finish before it calls the server. So the row is on disk before any network call starts. The row holds the client transfer ID, the payer account, the recipient, the amount as a Long in minor units (8000 cents), the status "pending", and a created time. The status only moves to success when the server's transfer record comes back.

more: A retry after a crash reads the pending row and reuses its client transfer ID, so the server can deduplicate instead of creating a second transfer.

turns.name: W3-change1
turns.question: Your sequence ends with "API-->>R: record status" and "VM-->>S: success," which assumes the response arrives. If the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process, what does A see on reopen, and how does the pending row get resolved? Please update your sequence diagram.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: Client layers (Screen, ViewModel, Repository, Local DB) talk to the server API, which owns the ledger; local DB caches balance and history and saves the transfer intent before sending
card.constraints: ["Start by clarifying the requirements", "MVP user path: a user sends money to a contact, then sees balance and history"]
card.heard: process killed, what does the app do on reopen, how is the pending row resolved
card.say: On reopen, the app reads the pending row from Room and shows "still checking", not success and not failure. The repository then asks the server for that transfer, using the account and the same client transfer ID. It never makes a new ID. If the server has the record, the app saves its status and shows the real result. If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight. So the row only leaves pending when the server's record says so. I'd resend that same client ID only while the server's idempotency window still covers it; after that, I'd rely on the lookup and reconciliation, never a new ID. The server answers a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's status, so the ledger still has only one transfer.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The users were travelers on the KKday app.
Candidate: They wanted to book tours and activities at their destination.
Candidate: Planning by hand was slow: work out the budget, search products one by one, then put the plan together.
Candidate: So the AI took a destination, a budget and a number of days, and built a trip they could book.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan: the agent design, the tools it calls, and the core backend.
Candidate: It ended at the app side, where I agreed the card format with the app team and wrote the code that reads the stream.

Interviewer: For the KKday AI trip planner, you said your responsibility started at the technical plan and ended at the app side reading the stream. Which exact pieces did you build yourself, and which parts did the team own?
Candidate: I built the agent design, the tools it calls, and the core backend myself.
Candidate: On Android, I wrote the code that reads the SSE stream and shows the day cards.
Candidate: The app team owned the other screens, like the product page and the map.
Candidate: The backend team owned the product and order services the agent calls.
Candidate: I agreed the card format with the app team, so both sides matched.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made was on the Android side, in the code that reads the stream.
Candidate: The user enters a destination, a budget and a number of days, then taps to plan the trip.
Candidate: The app sends that request and opens an SSE connection.
Candidate: Each event that arrives is one day card.
Candidate: I parse each event, check it, and add the card to a StateFlow.

Candidate: One trade-off is that if the connection drops mid-stream, the cards already shown stay on screen, so I surface a retry that resumes from the last received day rather than clearing the plan.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest bug was a day card that sometimes showed the wrong price.
Candidate: It only happened when two events arrived close together.
Candidate: I first suspected the backend was sending bad data.
Candidate: But the log showed the events were fine.
Candidate: The real cause was on my side: two events updated the same StateFlow at once, so one card got the other's price.
Candidate: I fixed it by applying each event in order on one coroutine.
Candidate: To test it, I replayed recorded streams with two events close together, and the price stayed correct.
Candidate: To catch it earlier, I'd add a test that feeds events out of order and checks each card keeps its own price.
Interviewer: You said the log showed the events were fine, but how did you confirm the race was actually in your StateFlow updates rather than somewhere else in the stream handling?
Candidate: I confirmed it by replaying recorded streams with two events close together.
Candidate: With the old code the price swapped; with the single coroutine it stayed correct.
Candidate: I also added a check that logs the event id and the card id together, so a mismatch shows up straight away.
Candidate: The replay only covers two events close together, so I'd also test a burst of many events in one frame.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: I had two other options.
Candidate: One was a mutex around the StateFlow update.
Candidate: The other was a single Channel that one consumer reads in order.
Candidate: I didn't pick the mutex because it still lets two events run in any order, so the price could still swap.
Candidate: I didn't pick the Channel because it adds a second buffer and more code for the same result.
Candidate: Its limit is that it only covers the cases we saw, so it can't prove there's no problem on devices or networks we didn't test.
Candidate: I also added a guard that drops any event whose card id no longer matches the current state, so a late event can't overwrite a newer price.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At Debon Securities, I was moving part of our trading app to the new navigation.
Candidate: During testing I found some old pages had a broken back button.
Candidate: I told the project manager that same day, before I had checked every page.
Candidate: I gave two options: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and test the rest after.
Candidate: He decided to keep the old pages, so everything else shipped on time.
Candidate: I finished the fix and the testing myself, and my change went out in the next release.
Candidate: If he had refused to delay, I'd have explained the risk clearly: which pages could break and for how many users.
Candidate: Then I'd ask for a quick way to turn the change off.
Candidate: The decision is his, but my job is to make the risk clear.
Candidate: The pages I found were older, low-traffic ones.
Candidate: If the broken back button had been on the checkout flow, I would have pushed harder to delay the release.
Candidate: I wouldn't have offered the ship-and-test-later option at all.
Interviewer: On the Debon navigation release, what risk were you willing to accept, who watched the data afterward, and what signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: I accepted the risk on those older, low-traffic pages.
Candidate: The main flow stayed on the old pages, so a broken back button there was annoying, not damaging.
Candidate: I wasn't willing to accept that risk on checkout, and I said so.
Candidate: After release, I watched the crash rate and the ANR rate in Bugly.
Candidate: I also watched support tickets about the back button.
Candidate: I'd set the watch up before the release, not after it.
Candidate: I'd agree the numbers with the PM first: crash rate, ANR rate, and back-button tickets per day.
Candidate: I'd also add a quick switch to turn the new navigation off.
Candidate: Then a bad signal means one action, not a long meeting.
Candidate: If the crash rate or the back-button tickets went above the agreed line, I'd pause the rollout and roll back that part.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: I'd define the MVP as one path: a user sends money to a contact, then sees their balance and history.

Candidate: I'd also assume the server ledger is the single source of truth for every balance, with the app only showing what the server confirms.

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the client as its layers, then the server and its ledger.
Candidate: The screen shows the balance and history and takes the user's confirm tap.
Candidate: The ViewModel holds the screen state and sends the transfer request.
Candidate: The repository is the only place that talks to the server.
Candidate: The local database keeps the cached balance and history, and it saves the transfer intent with its client transfer ID before we send anything.

Candidate: The local database saves the transfer intent with its client transfer ID before we send anything, so a retry after a dropped connection reuses that same ID and the server can reject the duplicate instead of applying the transfer twice.

Candidate: The server keeps one transfer record for that ID, and it answers a repeat with that record's current status.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: A sends 80 dollars, so that's 8000 cents.
Candidate: A confirms on the screen, and the ViewModel asks the repository to send it.
Candidate: The repository saves the intent with its client transfer ID in the local database first, then calls the server.
Candidate: The server checks and moves the money in one transaction: A goes from 100 to 20 dollars, B from 0 to 80.
Candidate: It writes one transfer record for that ID and returns the status.

Candidate: If the same ID comes again with the same amount and recipient, it doesn't move money twice; it just returns that record's current status.

Interviewer: You said the repository saves the intent with its client transfer ID in the local database before calling the server. On Android, how is that local write actually done so it's durable before the network call, and what exactly gets stored in that row?
Candidate: The repository writes the intent row to Room on the IO dispatcher, and it waits for that write to finish before it calls the server.
Candidate: So the row is on disk before any network call starts.
Candidate: The row holds the client transfer ID, the payer account, the recipient, the amount as a Long in minor units (8000 cents), the status "pending", and a created time.
Candidate: The status only moves to success when the server's transfer record comes back.

Interviewer: Your sequence ends with "API-->>R: record status" and "VM-->>S: success," which assumes the response arrives. If the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process, what does A see on reopen, and how does the pending row get resolved? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: On reopen, the app reads the pending row from Room and shows "still checking", not success and not failure.
Candidate: The repository then asks the server for that transfer, using the account and the same client transfer ID.
Candidate: It never makes a new ID.
Candidate: If the server has the record, the app saves its status and shows the real result.
Candidate: If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.
Candidate: So the row only leaves pending when the server's record says so.
